accuracy.evidence: Checked against Development Matters (3 and 4 year olds: say one number for each item in order 1-5; the last number reached tells how many in total, the cardinal principle; fast recognition of up to 3 without counting, subitising), the EYFS Number ELG (subitise up to 5) and Common Core K.CC.B.4a-b. The five counting principles are named as Gelman and Gallistel (1978) state them. Every lab total is right: 4 ducks, 5 frogs, 3/5/2 in the how-many rounds, 5 stars after every move, plates of 3, 2 and 4, dice patterns 1-5 with standard pip layouts.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-counting errors: double counting (the touch step refuses a duck that already has a number; challenge 'counts one ball two times'), skipping or repeating number words (bee-count options 1,2,4,5,6 and 1,2,3,3,4), reciting the list or recounting instead of giving the cardinal (prediction 'Count again to find out', challenge option '1, 2, 3, 4'), believing a spread-out row has more (move-step prediction and 6-star answer), and 'give me N' overshoot or grabbing all (plate check and challenge 'when the spoons run out').

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanics are counting itself: each thing moves into a numbered counted row exactly once, a how-many answer is taken only after a spoken count stops, stars are spread, squashed or dragged with the total re-asked each time, a give-me plate is filled one strawberry at a time with a check, and dice patterns test subitising. It is not the one-to-one counters visual (no cardinality, conservation or give-me tasks there); shingle gate passed against every flagship lab including flag_say and flag_match.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds that each duck gets one number and that a counted one cannot be counted again, hears a count stop and learns the last word is the answer, sees 5 stars stay 5 however they are arranged, discovers they must stop at the asked-for number, and then recognises small groups at a glance. The step text names each idea only after the child has tried it.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Count again to find out' when asked how many after counting 1,2,3 (the how-many step accepts the last number at once), and 'More than 5' after spreading the stars (the lab shows and checks it is still 5, with a 6 button that is rejected with a reason).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions and twelve tagged messages: reciting the list instead of the total, one counted twice, spread-out looks bigger, pushed-together looks smaller, double counting gives too few versus too many, running out instead of stopping, stopping one late, skipped number, repeated number, starting at the other end, and giving the first number said instead of the last.

readability.evidence: Kid text passes the family grade-5 limit with short sentences about ducks and spoons; canvas labels are a few words with emoji, and every canvas action has a big 56 px button. Adult text is under grade 10 and uses the exact terms one-to-one correspondence, stable order, cardinal principle, order irrelevance, abstraction and subitising.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and the 12% duplicate gate against every lesson including One-to-one counting and Saying number names in order. Each kid paragraph adds one idea (touch and say, one number each, last number is how many, arrangement and give-me); adult paragraphs give curriculum goals, the counting principles, the common mistakes and the lab outline.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 dark and 360 px Android light screenshots of all six steps: the four ducks and the counted row fit, the five number tiles sit in one row, the plate and basket sit side by side with readable labels, the dice is large and centred, and the young class gives 56 px buttons under the canvas with nothing clipped.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: every task completes with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge shows, axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes, no console errors. Each drag has a button route (count-this-duck buttons, number buttons, spread/squash/mix, put on/take off/that is it) and the canvas aria-label speaks each number word and the result after every move.

Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, K.CC.B.4a-b (one-to-one correspondence; the last number name said tells the number of objects counted)
